answer: Amber (Z-score) peaked in the 4th millennium BCE, reaching its maximum value of 1.54 over the interval 3300–3000 BCE. This 301-year plateau corresponds to four consecutive 100-year data bins (3300, 3200, 3100, and 3000 BCE) in the raw dataset, all sharing the identical maximum Z-score. The peak lies within the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE) for 300 of the 301 years and touches the 3rd millennium BCE by one year (3000 BCE) under strict millennium boundary conventions.

payload.hypothesis: Amber (Z-score) peaked in the 4th millennium BCE, at its maximum value of 1.54 over the interval 3300–3000 BCE (a 301-year plateau spanning four consecutive 100-year data bins).
payload.workflow: Loaded time_series_data.csv (3601 rows, 1-year resolution, CE −4100 to −500). Identified the global maximum of the Amber_inter column (1.54). Located the contiguous CE range at that maximum (CE −3300 to −3000, i.e., 3300–3000 BCE). Assigned the millennium using the convention Nth millennium BCE = N×1000 to N×1000−999 BCE: 3300 BCE falls in the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE); 3000 BCE falls in the 3rd millennium BCE (3000–2001 BCE). Confirmed 300 of 301 plateau years lie in the 4th millennium. Cross-checked against capital.csv Zamber column (100-year resolution): max = 1.54 at BCE 3300, 3200, 3100, 3000 — exact agreement. Verified interpolation is strictly linear with no overshoot beyond the raw data range.
